screens.title: Half Adders, Full Adders, and the ALU
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic is the foundation of every computation. In this chapter we start with the smallest building block, the half adder, and step-by-step build a full adder, a 16-bit ripple-carry adder, and finally the Hack ALU. You will learn the Boolean formulas that implement sum and carry, how to chain full adders to add multi-bit numbers, and how the ALU’s six control bits let a single unit perform addition, logical operations, negation, and constants. We’ll also cover the ALU’s two status flags, zero and negative, and why they matter for branching. A practical outcome is that you will be able to implement these chips in HDL and test them. Picture the ALU as a small control panel: switches preprocess inputs, a function stage computes either addition or bitwise and, and a post stage can negate the result. This matters because the ALU is the C P U’s computational heart — get these blocks right and everything above them works reliably. What happens when a carry must travel through many bits? We’ll explore that next.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Overview
Half Adders, Full Adders, and the ALU
Construct addition from gates and assemble the Hack ALU with control bits and flags.
In this lesson
Build half and full adders. Chain 16 full adders to make a ripple-carry adder. Implement the Hack ALU and verify its outputs and flags.
Why it matters
Every arithmetic operation in a CPU flows through these components. Understanding them gives you control over correctness and timing when building processors in HDL.
Explore Key Topics
Half & Full Adders
Single-bit arithmetic and composing adders with gates.
Ripple-Carry Adder
Chain full adders; understand carry propagation delay.
Hack ALU
Control bits, operations, and status flags used for branching.
Visual concept
Think of adders as small calculators. Each calculator produces a sum and may pass a carry to its neighbor. The ALU is a control panel that routes two 16-bit inputs through preprocessing, a function stage, and optional post-processing to produce the final output and flags.
Result
A compact ALU can perform many operations using a small set of control bits.
Caveat
Ripple-carry adders are simple but slow due to sequential carry propagation.
Getting ready
Have your HDL editor ready. Start by implementing the half adder, then the full adder, then Add16, and finally the ALU as specified in the project tasks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design and implement a half adder and a full adder using logic gates, chain full adders into a 16-bit ripple-carry adder, and understand the Hack ALU’s structure and control bits. You will also implement the Hack ALU in HDL and verify its operation. Each objective builds practical skills: the half adder teaches bit-level Boolean formulas like XOR and AND; the full adder shows how to incorporate a carry-in and compose smaller chips into larger ones. Building Add16 demonstrates how carries propagate and why delay matters. Finally, the ALU objective walks you through preprocessing inputs, selecting addition versus bitwise operations, post-processing by negation, and computing the zero and negative flags used for branching. You will test each chip with truth tables and sample inputs to validate behavior. These are essential competencies for constructing a functional C P U in HDL and for reasoning about timing and control in simple processor design.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Learning objectives include not just design but verification. You will write HDL tests for HalfAdder, FullAdder, Add16, and the ALU. For single-bit chips, truth tables exhaustively check behavior. For Add16 and the ALU, you will simulate representative inputs including edge cases: all zeros, all ones, carry chains, and negative values using two's complement representation. Verification teaches you to interpret outputs and status flags, especially the zero and negative signals. When testing the ALU, exercise control-bit combinations that produce constants like zero, one, and minus one. Practically, this means creating test vectors, running the HDL simulator, and checking that out, zr, and ng match expectations. If a test fails, trace signals back: check pre-processing (zeroing and negating inputs), function selection (add vs. and), and post-processing (negate output). This test-driven approach ensures the ALU works for all specified operations and supports branching logic in the C P U.

screens.title: Half Adder: Definition and Truth Table
screens.narratorSegment: A half adder is the simplest arithmetic building block: it adds two single bits and produces two outputs, a sum and a carry. Formally, the sum is the exclusive OR of the inputs, and the carry is their logical AND. Practically, when both inputs are 1, the sum becomes 0 and the carry becomes 1 — that carry is what moves to the next more significant bit in multi-bit addition. The truth table exhaustively lists the four input combinations and their results: 0+0 yields sum 0 carry 0; 0+1 or 1+0 yields sum 1 carry 0; 1+1 yields sum 0 carry 1. A common misconception is to expect the sum to be the arithmetic carry alone — instead, sum is the bit result after removing the carry, implemented by XOR. This difference matters when you compose adders: the full adder uses both XOR and AND outputs from half adders to include an incoming carry. For practice, compute by hand a few examples and confirm the half adder’s outputs always match the XOR and AND formulas. How would this change if you allowed a carry-in?

keyIdea.title: Half adder essence
keyIdea.text: Sum = a XOR b, Carry = a AND b. It lacks carry-in and so is the 'half' of a full adder.

content.html:
Core Concept Half Adder
Half Adder
A single-bit adder producing a sum and a carry. It cannot accept a carry-in.
Boolean formulas
Sum   = a XOR b
Carry = a AND b
Truth table
abSumCarry
0000
0110
1010
1101
Concrete example
Add bits a=1 and b=1. XOR yields 0 for the sum, AND yields 1 as a carry. That carry is what a full adder would accept as carry-in for the next bit.
Common misconception
Confusing the sum with carry. The sum is not the arithmetic total when a carry exists; the carry represents the overflow that must travel to a higher bit.
Key Takeaway

The half adder gives you XOR and AND outputs; use these to compose larger adders that handle carry-in.

screens.title: Implementing a Half Adder in Gates
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing a half adder uses two basic gates: XOR for the sum and AND for the carry. In HDL you express these formulas directly or use primitive gate chips. For practice, write the chip so that when inputs a and b change, the outputs update to sum = a XOR b and carry = a AND b. A concrete test vector: apply a=1, b=1 and expect sum 0 and carry 1. Another helpful test is a=0, b=1. Remember that XOR is true when inputs differ; AND is true only when both are 1. A typical mistake is to try to implement XOR by combining AND and OR carelessly—use the XOR primitive where available, or implement XOR as (a & ~b) | (~a & b) if your HDL requires it. Verify using a truth table in your simulator. This step connects Boolean definitions to practical HDL code and prepares you to compose half adders into full adders. After this implementation, you should be able to reason about each output for any input pair and catch errors by comparing to the truth table.

keyIdea.title: Implementation tip
keyIdea.text: Use XOR and AND primitives, or implement XOR as (a & ~b) | (~a & b) if needed. Always verify with truth vectors.

content.html:
Definition Half Adder Implementation
Implementing the logic
Choose an HDL form that maps cleanly to XOR and AND. Test exhaustively for correctness.
Example HDL-like code
// Pseudocode for clarity
CHIP HalfAdder {
  IN a, b;
  OUT sum, carry;

  sum   = a XOR b;
  carry = a AND b;
}
Test vectors
  • a=0 b=0 → sum=0 carry=0
  • a=1 b=0 → sum=1 carry=0
  • a=1 b=1 → sum=0 carry=1
Concrete example
When a=1 and b=0, XOR yields 1 and AND yields 0. The half adder outputs correspond to those gate results; no carry-in is considered.
Common mistake
Implementing XOR incorrectly by trying to reuse OR logic without handling exclusive cases. Use the XOR expression or its equivalent with NOT and ANDs.
Key Takeaway

Express XOR and AND clearly in HDL and verify with truth vectors before composing into larger adders.

screens.title: Full Adder: Three-bit Addition
screens.narratorSegment: A full adder extends the half adder by accepting a carry-in from a less-significant bit. Its boolean formulas capture three-input addition: the sum is the XOR of a, b, and the carry-in; the carry-out is true when a and b are both 1, or when the carry-in is 1 and exactly one of a or b is 1. This second term can be written as c AND (a XOR b), producing the full-carry expression: carry = (a AND b) OR (c AND (a XOR b)). The full adder truth table has eight rows; it describes every combination of a, b, and carry-in. Practically, this chip is the key to multi-bit addition because it propagates carries forward. A misconception is thinking the carry-out equals majority(a,b,c); while that matches numeric intuition, the standard expression shows how to implement carry using simpler gates and reusing XOR outputs. Understanding this formula is important when you translate the design into HDL or into two half adders plus an OR gate, which is the next topic. Full Adder: Three-bit Addition means full adder handles carry-in: sum = a xor b xor c; carry-out = (a and b) or (c and (a xor b)).. In practical terms, include carry-in: sum = a xor b xor c, carry = (a and b) or (c and (a xor b)). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Full adder essence
keyIdea.text: Full adder handles carry-in: Sum = a XOR b XOR c; Carry-out = (a AND b) OR (c AND (a XOR b)).

content.html:
Core Concept Full Adder
Full Adder formulas
Sum   = a XOR b XOR c
Carry = (a AND b) OR (c AND (a XOR b))
Truth table highlights
Eight input combinations determine sum and carry-out. For example, a=1, b=1, c=1 produces sum 1 and carry-out 1.
Concrete example
Add a=1, b=0, carry-in c=1. XORing gives sum = 0, and carry-out = 1 if either a&b or c&(a XOR b) is true. Here, c&(a XOR b) = 1, so carry-out = 1.
Misconception
Thinking carry-out is simply whether two or more inputs are 1 is numerically correct, but the standard implementation uses XOR and AND to reuse intermediate signals efficiently in hardware.
Key Takeaway

Full adders accept carry-in and produce carry-out, enabling multi-bit addition when chained.

screens.title: Building a Full Adder from Two Half Adders
screens.narratorSegment: You can implement a full adder by composing two half adders and an OR gate. First, the primary half adder adds a and b to produce sum1 and carry1. Then a second half adder adds sum1 and the incoming carry-in c to produce the final sum and carry2. Finally, the carry-out is the OR of carry1 and carry2. This decomposition is practical because it reuses the half adder design and keeps the logic modular. For example, if a=1, b=1, c=0: the first half adder yields sum1=0 carry1=1; the second half adder adds sum1 and c yielding sum=0 carry2=0; the OR of carry1 and carry2 gives carry-out=1. A common mistake is to forget to OR both carries, which loses cases where a and b produce a carry even if the second half adder’s carry2 is zero. Modular construction simplifies testing: verify each half adder separately, then verify their composition with the OR gate. This approach mirrors hardware design practices where small verified blocks are assembled into larger, testable units. Building a Full Adder from Two Half Adders means two half adders plus an or produce a full adder, enabling reuse and simpler verification.. In practical terms, compose smaller chips: halfadder(a,b) + halfadder(sum1,c) + or(carry1, carry2). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Composition pattern
keyIdea.text: Two half adders plus an OR produce a full adder, enabling reuse and simpler verification.

content.html:
Process Flow Full Adder from Half Adders
Step-by-step
  1. HalfAdder(a, b) → sum1, carry1
  2. HalfAdder(sum1, c) → sum, carry2
  3. carry-out = carry1 OR carry2
Worked example
a=1 b=1 c=0 → First half: sum1=0 carry1=1. Second half: sum=0 carry2=0. OR → carry-out=1.
Why reuse matters
Smaller verified blocks reduce engineering errors. If each half adder is correct, the composition is easier to trust and debug.
Common pitfall
Omitting the final OR step loses carry-out cases, causing wrong results when both lower bits produce carries.
Key Takeaway

Compose verified half adders and OR their carries to build a correct full adder with minimal new logic.

screens.title: Add16: The Ripple-Carry Adder
screens.narratorSegment: A 16-bit adder is constructed by connecting 16 full adders in series: each full adder computes one bit of the result and forwards its carry-out to the next more significant bit. The least significant bit uses a carry-in of zero. This structure is called a ripple-carry adder because carries move or 'ripple' through the chain as needed. In HDL, define Add16 to instantiate 16 FullAdder chips and wire the carry outputs to the next chip’s carry-in. A practical example: adding two 16-bit numbers where every lower bit generates carries will force the carry to traverse many stages before the most significant bit resolves. The ripple design is simple and area-efficient, making it suitable for educational CPUs like Hack. However, the sequential propagation of carry creates a delay proportional to the bit width. When debugging Add16, inspect the carry chain if outputs are wrong. Does any adder output an unexpected carry? Tracing that carry back to its origin is usually the fastest way to find the bug. Add16: The Ripple-Carry Adder means connect 16 full adders; carry-out of each becomes carry-in of the next. simple but introduces ripple delay.. In practical terms, chain 16 full adders so carries ripple from least to most significant bit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Add16 design
keyIdea.text: Connect 16 full adders; carry-out of each becomes carry-in of the next. Simple but introduces ripple delay.

content.html:
Architecture Add16 — Ripple-Carry
Chain layout
Add16(a[0..15], b[0..15]) produces out[0..15]. FullAdder at bit 0 takes carry-in 0. Each FullAdder(i) produces out[i] and carry[i], which feeds FullAdder(i+1).
FullAdder(a[0], b[0], 0) → out[0], carry[0]
FullAdder(a[1], b[1], carry[0]) → out[1], carry[1]
...
FullAdder(a[15], b[15], carry[14]) → out[15], carry[15]
Concrete scenario
If lower bits produce carries, the carry must propagate through each subsequent full adder, possibly changing many outputs before the MSB settles.
Verification note
Test patterns that force long carry chains to expose ripple behavior and timing issues in simulation.
Key Takeaway

Add16 is straightforward to implement and reason about, but carries cause sequential delay that impacts performance.

screens.title: Carry Propagation Delay and Alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Ripple-carry adders are simple, but their carry propagation delay grows with the number of bits. Each full adder must wait for the carry-in before producing a correct carry-out, so a 16-bit ripple adder can require up to 16 sequential full-adder delays. In practice, this means slower arithmetic at the C P U clock rates used in high-performance processors. The chapter mentions faster designs used in real processors: carry-lookahead adders compute generate and propagate signals to resolve carries in parallel, carry-select adders precompute sums for both possible carry-in values and then choose the correct result, and prefix adders use parallel prefix networks to compute carries more quickly. These designs trade logic complexity and area for speed. A common error is to assume more bits always mean only linear slow-down; with advanced adders the delay can be reduced to logarithmic depth. For the Hack computer we accept ripple-carry for simplicity and educational clarity. When you move to performance-sensitive designs, you will explore carry-lookahead and related patterns to reduce latency. Carry Propagation Delay and Alternatives means ripple-carry is simple but slow; faster adders trade area and complexity for lower carry delay using parallel carry computation or precomputation.. In practical terms, why ripple-carry is slow and what real processors use instead. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Delay trade-off
keyIdea.text: Ripple-carry is simple but slow; faster adders trade area and complexity for lower carry delay using parallel carry computation or precomputation.

content.html:
Comparison Delay: Ripple vs Faster Adders
Ripple-carry characteristics
  • Simple to implement by chaining full adders.
  • Delay grows linearly with bit width (O(n)).
  • Easy to verify and suitable for educational CPUs.
Faster alternatives (summary)
  • Carry-lookahead: compute carry signals in parallel using generate/propagate.
  • Carry-select: precompute sums for both carry-in values and select result.
  • Prefix adders: parallel prefix networks compute carries quickly.
Concrete performance point
If each full adder has delay D, Add16 can take up to 16·D in ripple form. Faster adders aim to reduce that to O(log n) depths at the cost of more gates.
Design trade-off
Accept ripple-carry for clarity and area, or invest in complex logic for speed. The Hack CPU chooses simplicity for learning.
Key Takeaway

Understand the carry-delay trade-off: simplicity versus speed guides adder selection in CPU design.

screens.title: The Hack ALU: Overview and Structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack ALU is designed as a compact, flexible 16-bit arithmetic-logic unit. It accepts two 16-bit inputs x and y, produces a 16-bit out, and outputs two status bits: zr (true if out is zero) and ng (true if out is negative, i. e., MSB = 1). Six control bits govern its behavior: zx and nx control preprocessing of x; zy and ny control preprocessing of y; f selects the function (addition when f=1, bitwise AND when f=0); and no negates the final output. Conceptually the ALU has stages: input preprocessing (zeroing or bitwise negation), a function stage that either adds or ANDs the processed inputs, and an output post-stage that may negate the result. This staged design makes the control bits powerful: by combining simple operations we obtain constants and unary operations in addition to binary ones. For implementation, structure your HDL into these stages so you can test each separately: preprocessors, function block, postprocessor, then flags. Why is staging helpful? It isolates faults and makes testing more systematic. keyIdea.title: ALU staging
keyIdea.text: Design the ALU in preprocessing, function selection, and postprocessing stages for clarity and testability.

content.html:
Core Concept Hack ALU Overview
ALU signature
Inputs: x[15..0], y[15..0], zx, nx, zy, ny, f, no. Outputs: out[15..0], zr, ng.
Operation stages
  1. Preprocessing: apply zx/nx to x, zy/ny to y.
  2. Function stage: if f=1 compute add, else compute bitwise AND.
  3. Postprocessing: apply no to negate the result if requested.
Concrete example
To compute x + y, leave zx/zy and nx/ny cleared, set f=1, and no=0. The function stage performs the addition, and flags reflect the result.
Design advice
Implement and test each stage separately: preprocessing units, add/and blocks, and the final negation, then compute flags from the final output.
Key Takeaway

The ALU uses simple control bits to combine small operations into many useful functions; staging simplifies implementation and testing.

screens.title: ALU Control Bits: zx, nx, zy, ny, f, no
screens.narratorSegment: The six ALU control bits let you transform inputs and the result to obtain a wide palette of functions. zx zeroes x when set; nx negates x after zeroing if requested. Zy and ny do the same for y. The f bit selects between the adder (f=1) and the bitwise AND (f=0). The no bit negates the ALU output at the end. These bits are independent stages: preprocessing, function selection, post-processing. Because each bit controls a specific stage rather than encoding a full operation, many distinct functions arise from combinations of bits. For example, clearing zx and zy and setting f=1 produces x+y. Zeroing both inputs and using f=1 or f=0 can produce constants like 0. A typical pitfall is thinking the bits encode functions as a binary opcode; instead, treat them as switches on pipeline stages. When you implement the ALU, ensure the bits apply in the correct sequence: zx/zy first, then nx/ny, then function, then no. Testing each control bit independently helps isolate errors when a complex combination fails. keyIdea.text: Each bit controls a specific stage; combine them to create multiple functions rather than interpreting them as a simple opcode.

content.html:
Definition ALU Control Bits
Control bits behavior
  • zx: if 1, set x = 0
  • nx: if 1, set x = NOT(x)
  • zy: if 1, set y = 0
  • ny: if 1, set y = NOT(y)
  • f: if 1 compute x+y, else compute x&y
  • no: if 1, set out = NOT(out)
Sequencing matters
Apply zx/zy, then nx/ny, then function f, then no. Incorrect order yields wrong results for many combinations.
Concrete examples
x+y: zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=0 f=1 no=0. To compute constants, zero and manipulate inputs before function selection.
Common error
Treating control bits as a function code. Instead, they should be seen as independent switches that change intermediate signals.
Key Takeaway

Control bits are stage switches. Combine preprocessing, function selection, and postprocessing to produce many useful ALU functions.

screens.title: ALU Operation Examples: x + y and x - y
screens.narratorSegment: To compute x + y the ALU uses simple control-bit values: leave zx, nx, zy, and ny cleared so inputs pass through unchanged, set f to 1 to select addition, and leave no cleared. The ALU then computes the 16-bit sum and the flags based on that result. Subtraction x - y is more subtle: arithmetic subtraction is x + (-y). Two's complement negation of y is ~y + 1. The Hack ALU achieves subtraction by using combinations of the control bits that effectively produce -y inside the function stage and then add it to x. The chapter notes the ALU pre-computes two's complement-like behavior internally; the precise control-word for x - y is given in the specification for implementation. A common confusion is assuming you can implement subtraction with only a simple negate bit; remember negating y alone gives ~y, not ~y + 1. Test subtraction with known pairs and watch the sign and zero flags to confirm correctness. When implementing, break the operation into preprocessing, function block, and postprocessing so you can isolate mistakes. ALU Operation Examples: x + y and x - y means x - y requires converting y to its two's complement form before addition; verify with sign and zero flags.. keyIdea.text: x - y requires converting y to its two's complement form before addition; verify with sign and zero flags.

content.html:
Process Flow Examples: x+y and x-y
x + y control bits
Set zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=0 f=1 no=0 so x and y pass unchanged and are added.
x - y concept
Subtraction uses x + (-y). The ALU implements negation and addition combination internally; you must ensure the two's complement behavior (~y + 1) is realized by the control sequence described in the specification.
Test case
// Example check
x = 0000 0000 0000 0010 (2)
y = 0000 0000 0000 0001 (1)
Expect x - y = 1, sign bit 0, zr = 0
Misconception
Negating y alone gives bitwise NOT, not arithmetic negative. Two's complement requires adding one after inversion to get -y.
Key Takeaway

Follow the ALU specification to realize subtraction; test with signed values and inspect flags to confirm correct two's complement behavior.

screens.title: ALU Status Flags: zr and ng
screens.narratorSegment: The ALU reports two status flags used by the C P U for conditional branching: zr indicates whether the output is all zeros, and ng indicates whether the output is negative by checking the most significant bit. Zero detection is implemented by reducing the 16-bit output to a single signal: perform an OR across all bits (often via an Or8Way on halves and then combine) and then invert the result; if no bit is 1, the OR yields 0 and the Not yields 1, setting zr. Negative detection is simpler: in two's complement a negative number has the most significant bit set, so ng equals the MSB of the output. These flags must be computed after all preprocessing and postprocessing on the output is complete. A mistake is computing flags before the final negation stage, which yields incorrect branch decisions. When testing, include vectors that produce zero and negative results to confirm both flags behave as expected. These tiny signals drive the C P U's jump logic and determine program flow, so they must be reliable. ALU Status Flags: zr and ng means compute zr by or-ing all output bits then not-ing; compute ng from the msb. flags must reflect the final out value.. In practical terms, detect zero output and negative result using bit operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flag logic
keyIdea.text: Compute zr by OR-ing all output bits then NOT-ing; compute ng from the MSB. Flags must reflect the final out value.

content.html:
Core Concept ALU Flags
Zero detection (zr)
Compute OR across all sixteen output bits. If the OR is 0, invert it to produce zr=1. Common implementation uses Or8Way on both halves, then OR and NOT to finalize zr.
Negative detection (ng)
In two's complement, negative numbers have MSB = 1. Set ng equal to out[15] to signal negativity.
Concrete example
If out = 0000 0000 0000 0000 then OR = 0 → NOT → zr = 1. If out[15] = 1, ng = 1 indicating a negative result.
Common pitfall
Computing flags before final negation or postprocessing leads to wrong branch behavior. Always compute flags from the final out value.
Key Takeaway

Reliable zero and negative flags are essential for correct control flow. Derive them from the final output after all ALU stages.

What to Remember
Half Adder
Sum = a XOR b; Carry = a AND b. No carry-in support.
Full Adder
Handles carry-in: Sum = a XOR b XOR c; Carry-out = (a&b) OR (c&(a XOR b)).

Chain 16 full adders. Simple to build, but carry delay is linear in bit width.

fullNarratorScript:
Arithmetic is the foundation of every computation. In this chapter we start with the smallest building block, the half adder, and step-by-step build a full adder, a 16-bit ripple-carry adder, and finally the Hack ALU. You will learn the Boolean formulas that implement sum and carry, how to chain full adders to add multi-bit numbers, and how the ALU’s six control bits let a single unit perform addition, logical operations, negation, and constants. We’ll also cover the ALU’s two status flags, zero and negative, and why they matter for branching. A practical outcome is that you will be able to implement these chips in HDL and test them. Picture the ALU as a small control panel: switches preprocess inputs, a function stage computes either addition or bitwise and, and a post stage can negate the result. This matters because the ALU is the C P U’s computational heart — get these blocks right and everything above them works reliably. What happens when a carry must travel through many bits? We’ll explore that next.

By the end of this chapter you will design and implement a half adder and a full adder using logic gates, chain full adders into a 16-bit ripple-carry adder, and understand the Hack ALU’s structure and control bits. You will also implement the Hack ALU in HDL and verify its operation. Each objective builds practical skills: the half adder teaches bit-level Boolean formulas like XOR and AND; the full adder shows how to incorporate a carry-in and compose smaller chips into larger ones. Building Add16 demonstrates how carries propagate and why delay matters. Finally, the ALU objective walks you through preprocessing inputs, selecting addition versus bitwise operations, post-processing by negation, and computing the zero and negative flags used for branching. You will test each chip with truth tables and sample inputs to validate behavior. These are essential competencies for constructing a functional C P U in HDL and for reasoning about timing and control in simple processor design.

Learning objectives include not just design but verification. You will write HDL tests for HalfAdder, FullAdder, Add16, and the ALU. For single-bit chips, truth tables exhaustively check behavior. For Add16 and the ALU, you will simulate representative inputs including edge cases: all zeros, all ones, carry chains, and negative values using two's complement representation. Verification teaches you to interpret outputs and status flags, especially the zero and negative signals. When testing the ALU, exercise control-bit combinations that produce constants like zero, one, and minus one. Practically, this means creating test vectors, running the HDL simulator, and checking that out, zr, and ng match expectations. If a test fails, trace signals back: check pre-processing (zeroing and negating inputs), function selection (add vs. and), and post-processing (negate output). This test-driven approach ensures the ALU works for all specified operations and supports branching logic in the C P U.

A half adder is the simplest arithmetic building block: it adds two single bits and produces two outputs, a sum and a carry. Formally, the sum is the exclusive OR of the inputs, and the carry is their logical AND. Practically, when both inputs are 1, the sum becomes 0 and the carry becomes 1 — that carry is what moves to the next more significant bit in multi-bit addition. The truth table exhaustively lists the four input combinations and their results: 0+0 yields sum 0 carry 0; 0+1 or 1+0 yields sum 1 carry 0; 1+1 yields sum 0 carry 1. A common misconception is to expect the sum to be the arithmetic carry alone — instead, sum is the bit result after removing the carry, implemented by XOR. This difference matters when you compose adders: the full adder uses both XOR and AND outputs from half adders to include an incoming carry. For practice, compute by hand a few examples and confirm the half adder’s outputs always match the XOR and AND formulas. How would this change if you allowed a carry-in?

Implementing a half adder uses two basic gates: XOR for the sum and AND for the carry. In HDL you express these formulas directly or use primitive gate chips. For practice, write the chip so that when inputs a and b change, the outputs update to sum = a XOR b and carry = a AND b. A concrete test vector: apply a=1, b=1 and expect sum 0 and carry 1. Another helpful test is a=0, b=1. Remember that XOR is true when inputs differ; AND is true only when both are 1. A typical mistake is to try to implement XOR by combining AND and OR carelessly—use the XOR primitive where available, or implement XOR as (a & ~b) | (~a & b) if your HDL requires it. Verify using a truth table in your simulator. This step connects Boolean definitions to practical HDL code and prepares you to compose half adders into full adders. After this implementation, you should be able to reason about each output for any input pair and catch errors by comparing to the truth table.

A full adder extends the half adder by accepting a carry-in from a less-significant bit. Its boolean formulas capture three-input addition: the sum is the XOR of a, b, and the carry-in; the carry-out is true when a and b are both 1, or when the carry-in is 1 and exactly one of a or b is 1. This second term can be written as c AND (a XOR b), producing the full-carry expression: carry = (a AND b) OR (c AND (a XOR b)). The full adder truth table has eight rows; it describes every combination of a, b, and carry-in. Practically, this chip is the key to multi-bit addition because it propagates carries forward. A misconception is thinking the carry-out equals majority(a,b,c); while that matches numeric intuition, the standard expression shows how to implement carry using simpler gates and reusing XOR outputs. Understanding this formula is important when you translate the design into HDL or into two half adders plus an OR gate, which is the next topic. Full Adder: Three-bit Addition means full adder handles carry-in: sum = a xor b xor c; carry-out = (a and b) or (c and (a xor b)).. In practical terms, include carry-in: sum = a xor b xor c, carry = (a and b) or (c and (a xor b)). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

You can implement a full adder by composing two half adders and an OR gate. First, the primary half adder adds a and b to produce sum1 and carry1. Then a second half adder adds sum1 and the incoming carry-in c to produce the final sum and carry2. Finally, the carry-out is the OR of carry1 and carry2. This decomposition is practical because it reuses the half adder design and keeps the logic modular. For example, if a=1, b=1, c=0: the first half adder yields sum1=0 carry1=1; the second half adder adds sum1 and c yielding sum=0 carry2=0; the OR of carry1 and carry2 gives carry-out=1. A common mistake is to forget to OR both carries, which loses cases where a and b produce a carry even if the second half adder’s carry2 is zero. Modular construction simplifies testing: verify each half adder separately, then verify their composition with the OR gate. This approach mirrors hardware design practices where small verified blocks are assembled into larger, testable units. Building a Full Adder from Two Half Adders means two half adders plus an or produce a full adder, enabling reuse and simpler verification.. In practical terms, compose smaller chips: halfadder(a,b) + halfadder(sum1,c) + or(carry1, carry2). A 16-bit adder is constructed by connecting 16 full adders in series: each full adder computes one bit of the result and forwards its carry-out to the next more significant bit. The least significant bit uses a carry-in of zero. This structure is called a ripple-carry adder because carries move or 'ripple' through the chain as needed. In HDL, define Add16 to instantiate 16 FullAdder chips and wire the carry outputs to the next chip’s carry-in. A practical example: adding two 16-bit numbers where every lower bit generates carries will force the carry to traverse many stages before the most significant bit resolves. The ripple design is simple and area-efficient, making it suitable for educational CPUs like Hack. However, the sequential propagation of carry creates a delay proportional to the bit width. When debugging Add16, inspect the carry chain if outputs are wrong. Does any adder output an unexpected carry? Tracing that carry back to its origin is usually the fastest way to find the bug. Ripple-carry adders are simple, but their carry propagation delay grows with the number of bits. Each full adder must wait for the carry-in before producing a correct carry-out, so a 16-bit ripple adder can require up to 16 sequential full-adder delays. In practice, this means slower arithmetic at the C P U clock rates used in high-performance processors. The chapter mentions faster designs used in real processors: carry-lookahead adders compute generate and propagate signals to resolve carries in parallel, carry-select adders precompute sums for both possible carry-in values and then choose the correct result, and prefix adders use parallel prefix networks to compute carries more quickly. These designs trade logic complexity and area for speed. A common error is to assume more bits always mean only linear slow-down; with advanced adders the delay can be reduced to logarithmic depth. For the Hack computer we accept ripple-carry for simplicity and educational clarity. When you move to performance-sensitive designs, you will explore carry-lookahead and related patterns to reduce latency. The Hack ALU is designed as a compact, flexible 16-bit arithmetic-logic unit. It accepts two 16-bit inputs x and y, produces a 16-bit out, and outputs two status bits: zr (true if out is zero) and ng (true if out is negative, i. e., MSB = 1). Six control bits govern its behavior: zx and nx control preprocessing of x; zy and ny control preprocessing of y; f selects the function (addition when f=1, bitwise AND when f=0); and no negates the final output. Conceptually the ALU has stages: input preprocessing (zeroing or bitwise negation), a function stage that either adds or ANDs the processed inputs, and an output post-stage that may negate the result. This staged design makes the control bits powerful: by combining simple operations we obtain constants and unary operations in addition to binary ones. For implementation, structure your HDL into these stages so you can test each separately: preprocessors, function block, postprocessor, then flags. Why is staging helpful? The six ALU control bits let you transform inputs and the result to obtain a wide palette of functions. zx zeroes x when set; nx negates x after zeroing if requested. Zy and ny do the same for y. The f bit selects between the adder (f=1) and the bitwise AND (f=0). The no bit negates the ALU output at the end. These bits are independent stages: preprocessing, function selection, post-processing. Because each bit controls a specific stage rather than encoding a full operation, many distinct functions arise from combinations of bits. For example, clearing zx and zy and setting f=1 produces x+y. Zeroing both inputs and using f=1 or f=0 can produce constants like 0. A typical pitfall is thinking the bits encode functions as a binary opcode; instead, treat them as switches on pipeline stages. When you implement the ALU, ensure the bits apply in the correct sequence: zx/zy first, then nx/ny, then function, then no. The ALU reports two status flags used by the C P U for conditional branching: zr indicates whether the output is all zeros, and ng indicates whether the output is negative by checking the most significant bit. Zero detection is implemented by reducing the 16-bit output to a single signal: perform an OR across all bits (often via an Or8Way on halves and then combine) and then invert the result; if no bit is 1, the OR yields 0 and the Not yields 1, setting zr. Negative detection is simpler: in two's complement a negative number has the most significant bit set, so ng equals the MSB of the output. These flags must be computed after all preprocessing and postprocessing on the output is complete. A mistake is computing flags before the final negation stage, which yields incorrect branch decisions. When testing, include vectors that produce zero and negative results to confirm both flags behave as expected. These tiny signals drive the C P U's jump logic and determine program flow, so they must be reliable.
